title: Menemen
subtitle: Turkish scrambled eggs with tomato and pepper
excerpt: Menemen is the Turkish breakfast dish of eggs cooked directly in a pan of softened tomatoes and green peppers with olive oil. It is looser and juicier than scrambled eggs: the eggs are stirred gently into the tomato mixture as it sets, not cooked dry.
sourceNotes: Aylin Oney Tan, A Taste of Sun and Fire: Gaziantep Cookery (2014). Menemen documented as a staple of Turkish morning tables. Claudia Roden, Arabesque (2005). Turkish egg dishes including menemen described in the context of regional breakfast culture.

content.text: Menemen is eggs cooked in a pan of slowly softened tomatoes and peppers, stirred gently until the eggs just set in soft, silky folds. It is a Turkish breakfast dish and takes fifteen minutes from start to finish. The pan goes straight to the table and is eaten with bread for scooping. The eggs should not be overcooked: menemen is meant to be slightly custardy at the centre, not dried out.
Heat {{olive-oil}} in a wide frying pan over a medium-low heat. If using {{onion}}, add it now and cook for five minutes until soft. Add {{pepper-green}} and cook for five minutes until softened.
Add {{tomato}} and {{chilli-flakes}} if using. Stir and cook for six to eight minutes until the tomatoes have collapsed into a thick, jammy sauce. Season generously with salt and black pepper.

Crack {{eggs}} directly into the pan. Stir gently with a wooden spoon or spatula, drawing the egg through the tomato mixture in slow, wide strokes. Cook for two to three minutes until the eggs are just set but still loose and custardy. Remove from the heat while they look slightly underdone: they will finish cooking in the residual heat of the pan.
Scatter {{parsley-flat}} over if using and serve directly from the pan with bread.

items.symptom: The eggs are rubbery and overcooked
items.cause: Cooked for too long or over too high a heat
items.fix: Remove the pan from the heat when the eggs still look slightly underdone. They finish in the residual heat. Menemen should be soft and just set.

items.symptom: The mixture is watery rather than thick
items.cause: Tomatoes were not cooked down long enough
items.fix: Cook the tomatoes until they have reduced to a thick sauce before adding the eggs. The base should be jammy, not liquid.

items.cause: Not cooked long enough before the tomatoes were added
items.fix: Green peppers need at least five minutes of gentle cooking before they soften. Do not rush this step.

items.cause: Under-seasoned or tomatoes were not ripe enough
items.fix: Use the ripest, most flavourful tomatoes you can find. Season generously at the tomato stage, before adding the eggs.

content.text: Menemen is the most typical Turkish breakfast dish, eaten from Istanbul to the coast to the interior. Like most well-loved simple dishes, it generates strong opinions: whether to add onion is a real debate (some say it is not traditional; most home cooks use them), and whether the eggs should be stirred or left whole is another. The name is thought to come from a town in the Izmir region of western Turkey. In Turkish breakfast culture, menemen is part of a wide spread that includes cheeses, olives, bread, honey, clotted cream, and tomato, but it is also a good quick meal on its own.
